abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: This study presents a strategy for in situ chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell engineering using anti-CD5-conjugated lipid nanoparticles with mRNA encoding for a Positron emission tomography (PET) surface protein tag. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) expression was detected with PET/Computed Tomography (CT) imaging using 68Ga-PSMA-617, and engineered T cell trafficking was quantified. Based on the imaging methods, we optimized several aspects of in situ T cell engineering. The optimized protocol for in situ CAR-T therapy had significant antitumor activity. This paper highlights the potential role for PSMA-targeted PET imaging to provide monitoring capabilities for protocol development for in situ CAR-T cell therapy.

In situ T cell transfection methods overcome the complexity and high costs associated with conventional chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T therapy. However, the in situ CAR-T cell approach operates within the patient’s complex immune environment and bypasses preinfusion ex vivo cellular quality controls, necessitating advanced imaging techniques to track immune cell migration and function. Positron emission tomography (PET) can detect biochemical processes in patients and, when combined with a radiotracer specific for the engineered cells, can monitor CAR-T cell trafficking. Herein, we develop an approach for in situ T cell generation, tracking, and functional assessment using anti-CD5-conjugated lipid nanoparticles for codelivering CD19 CAR mRNA (mCAR19) and a prostate-specific membrane antigen mRNA (mPSMA) tag. With interleukin-7 (IL-7) preconditioning and repeated administration, this approach achieves tumor-free survival in 75% of B cell lymphoma-bearing mice (similar efficacy to ex vivo approaches), and through PET imaging of 68Ga-PSMA-617, the generation and tumor infiltration of in situ-engineered PSMA-tagged CD19 CAR-T cells is validated.

body.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has revolutionized the treatment of hematological malignancies over the past years, demonstrating impressive response rates and durable remission for patients (1). Conventional CAR-T cell therapy is not only time consuming but also has significant costs (2). The ex vivo process poses additional challenges in the risk of contamination and loss of cell viability, and requires extensive infrastructure (3). Alternatively, systemic administration of viral and nonviral vectors produces CAR-T cells within the patient’s body. This approach not only reduces the time between T cell modification and treatment (3), but also minimizes the risks of immune rejection from adoptive cells and contamination from complex ex vivo engineering. However, unlike conventional CAR-T cell therapy, the in situ approach operates within the patient’s complex immune environment, and bypasses preinfusion ex vivo cellular quality controls and assessment for the generated CAR-T cells (4).

Incorporating imaging in the development of in situ therapies has the potential to avoid current bottlenecks. First, efficient in situ CAR-T cell generation requires gene delivery to T cell dense lymphoid organs. Second, off-target effects resulting from increased dose or hepatic tropism of nanotherapies can increase toxicity and reduce efficacy. Third, since the efficiency and limited toxicity of nonviral vectors provide an opportunity for repeated administration, there is both the need and opportunity to repeatedly administer such therapies to achieve similar efficacy to ex vivo CAR-T generation protocols. Fourth, formulation with one or more gene constructs, required to achieve both imaging and therapy, must be optimized (5). Current monitoring methods for in situ CAR-T therapy involve harvesting tumors and lymphoid organs for ex vivo analysis. These endpoint monitoring methods cannot overcome the hurdles above and are not translational (6, 7).

Image-guided gene and cell therapy represents a promising approach in precision medicine. Current studies have labeled the transfection vectors themselves (8), or combined the vectors with imaging reporter genes to indicate the efficiency and specificity of the therapeutic gene expression (9) in order to monitor conventionally infused CAR-T cells (10). Optical imaging approaches are commonly used to visualize T cells in cell and animal models using mCherry, green fluorescent protein (GFP), or luciferase (Luc) as reporter genes, but these optical approaches are not suitable for clinical use in patients. In contrast, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging offers substantial benefits for active surveillance and analysis of cell activity in the clinic (11). PET allows visualization of trafficking of vectors such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) in vivo (12, 13), as well as tracking the location, expression, and persistence of the gene of interest by using viral vectors (14, 15) or cationic lipids (16) to codeliver both the target gene and PET reporter gene. However, image-guided monitoring, including PET, has not yet been applied to in situ CAR-T cell therapy.

PET imaging provides the potential to noninvasively track the distribution and tumor infiltration of ex vivo engineered CAR-T cells with higher sensitivity to specific targets (17). PET imaging agents targeted to prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) are becoming widely available for diagnostics and radiotheranostics (18). We propose using this antigen and imaging probe to optimize in situ CAR-T cell protocols. PSMA is a human protein with restricted normal tissue expression, and as reported, the tPSMA (N9del) variant lacks the putative intracellular signaling motifs, making it less likely to affect normal T cell function (19, 20). Approved PSMA-targeted probes include 18F-DCFPyL (PYLARIFY®, 2021) and 68Ga-PSMA-11 (LOCAMETZ®, 2022) (18), enabling the widespread use of PSMA-targeted PET imaging for in situ CAR-T cell surveillance in future clinical applications.

Among the various gene delivery methods for in situ CAR-T cell generation, nonviral vectors, such as LNPs encapsulating mRNA (LNP-mRNA) technology (21, 22), offer a scalable alternative to viral vectors, such as lentiviral vectors (LVs), which are often limited by safety concerns and production complexities. LNP-mRNA technology underlies recent successes in vaccine development (23) and holds exceptional promise for additional therapeutic strategies in oncology (24). Moreover, LNPs can be conjugated with targeting antibodies to direct internalization and mRNA expression to T cells specifically in situ (25). We selected CD19 as the specific CAR for these studies as there is established efficacy for treating CD19+ B cell lymphoma based on ex vivo T cell transfection (26). Our protocol is designed to provide a direct comparison with ex vivo CD19 CAR-T cell therapy in a syngeneic B cell lymphoma murine model (27, 28). Furthermore, given that a CAR-T cell population including both CD4+ and CD8+ cells enhances the antitumor efficacy (29), targeting both populations is desirable. For in situ CAR-T cell approaches, CD5 is a promising target, as it is expressed by T cells and a minor subset of B cells, and has limited impact on T cell functionalities (30, 31). CD5 ligation or reduction of CD5 levels by blockade (32) or knock-out (33) has been shown to activate T cells and enhance T cell cytotoxicity; additionally, CD5 deletion synergizes with adoptive T cell therapies (34). Therefore, CD5 targeting was selected for the LNP delivery system for treating B cell lymphoma in this study.

Herein, we develop an approach to monitor mRNA-based T cell transfection in situ after systemic injection using anti-CD5 antibody (aCD5) conjugated LNPs with interleukin-7 (IL-7) preconditioning (Fig. 1A). To address the challenges of in situ CAR-T cell therapy, we coformulated PSMA mRNA (mPSMA) with CD19 CAR mRNA (mCAR19) in the same LNPs to provide a PET imaging tag, simultaneously allowing us to track the generation and migration of the in situ-engineered CAR-T cells using 68Ga-PSMA-617, which binds to the expressed PSMA protein. We specifically set out to determine whether coadministration of the imaging and therapeutic mRNA packaged within a single LNP can achieve both effective therapy and image guidance, and whether multiple administrations of IL-7 and LNPs sustain repeated T cell transfection and achieve similar efficacy to reported ex vivo CAR-T protocols (27, 28). We hypothesize that repeated dosing of aCD5 LNPs directed to T lymphocytes will produce an efficacious CAR-T cell therapy against B cell lymphoma, and PSMA-targeted PET imaging will facilitate evaluation of the distribution of CAR-T cells, thereby optimizing the therapeutic efficacy.

sec.title: Engineered LNPs Enhance Splenic T Cell Transfection In Vitro and In Naïve BALB/c Mice.
sec.p: Clinically relevant ionizable lipids to deliver mRNA to immune cells were first compared in in vitro assays. A series of aCD5-targeted LNPs, including Lipid8, ALC-0315, Lipid5, DLin, C12-200, or 18PA DLin were prepared, and Fluc mRNA (mFLuc) was used as the reporter gene (SI Appendix, Table S1). All LNPs, regardless of their formulations, had a hydrodynamic diameter ranging from 100 to 120 nm, with a polydispersity index (PDI) of approximately 0.2 (SI Appendix, Table S2 and Fig. S1). In murine T cell lymphoma EL4 cells (SI Appendix, Fig. S2), the highest Fluc expression at 24 h after incubation was obtained with aCD5-targeted Lipid8 LNPs (P < 0.001). By comparison, in a CD5- mouse T cell line (TK-1), low levels of LNP binding and mRNA expression were observed (SI Appendix, Fig. S3).

For all in vivo studies of gene delivery, interleukin-7 (IL-7) was injected intraperitoneally (i.p.) prior to intravenous (i.v.) LNP administration (SI Appendix, Tables S3 and S4 and Fig. 1B) as IL-7 is a homeostatic cytokine that enhances T cell internalization of exogeneous gene constructs and enriches the pathways associated with protein translation in T cells (35). IL-7 has previously been used to prime T cells before in vivo LV transfection (36–38), and a recently published study also demonstrated that IL-7 increased LNP-mediated mCherry mRNA expression in T cells in vitro and in vivo (35). IL-7 has also been safely applied in clinical studies (39).

To evaluate the in vivo spleen tropism of LNP-mRNA delivery and transfection, aCD5 LNP-mFluc was intravenously injected into naïve BALB/c mice to track in vivo and ex vivo bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signal (Fig. 1C). Across a dosage range of 7 to 30 µg of mRNA per mouse, splenic accumulation at 5 h was greatest at a dose of 7 µg, while still maintaining a lower off-target liver accumulation (SI Appendix, Table S5). Positive FLuc expression was observed in lymphoid organs, particularly in the spleen with a peak at 3 to 5 h (P = 0.0060) (Fig. 1 C and D and SI Appendix, Figs. S4 and S5). Since mRNA expression is transient (40), the BLI signal decreased at 24 h. By comparison, for immunoglobulin G isotype-conjugated LNPs (IgG LNPs), BLI signal was primarily enhanced in the liver (Fig. 1E). Compared to the nontreated control spleen and IgG LNP-treated spleen, only the spleen treated with aCD5 LNP-mFluc showed positive Fluc expression upon IHC, while the spatial distribution of CD4+ and CD8+ cells remained unchanged, and the tissue morphology was unaffected upon H&E staining (Fig. 1F).

Therefore, aCD5-targeted LNPs containing Lipid8, with IL-7 preconditioning, efficiently delivered genes to T cells in secondary lymphoid organs with splenic transfection exceeding that in the liver with the 7-µg dose. The resulting LNPs were then evaluated for in situ CAR-T cell engineering.

sec.title: PET/CT Imaging Monitors PSMA-Tagged CAR-T Cells In Vitro and In Naïve BALB/c Mice.
sec.p: To evaluate the feasibility detecting CAR-T cells by inducing PSMA expression, murine T cell lymphoma EL4 cells were treated with aCD5 LNPs encapsulating mPSMA or mCAR19 alone, premixed mPSMA/mCAR19 (1:1), or a dose of separate aCD5 LNPs containing each mRNA (matching μg of each mRNA with a resultant increase in the LNP carrier mass) (SI Appendix, Table S6 and Fig. 2A). After 24 h, the aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 group (each LNP contains both mRNA) exhibited high coexpression of PSMA and CAR19 with 43.2% of cells double-positive and 61.1% of cells expressing CAR19 (Fig. 2B and SI Appendix, Fig. S6A). The individual protein expression was comparable to that of samples treated by aCD5 LNP-mPSMA or -mCAR19 alone. In contrast, the double-positive population was only 4.9% in cells treated with the mRNAs in separate LNPs (Fig. 2C and SI Appendix, Fig. S6A), due to the stochasticity of LNP uptake and mRNA endosomal escape (41). The results indicate that aCD5 LNPs enabled coencapsulation of both mPSMA and mCAR19 and achieved the greatest fraction of cells with coexpression of both mRNAs.

sec.p: Next, PSMA expression levels were evaluated for each LNP treatment group in EL4 cells and compared to that found in untreated EL4 cells (NTC) and baseline PSMA levels in PSMA-positive (LNCaP) and PSMA-negative (PPC-1) human prostate cancer cell lines. EL4 cells treated with aCD5 LNP-mPSMA or with LNPs coencapsulating both mPSMA and mCAR19 exhibited elevated PSMA expression levels, with median fluorescence intensities (MFIs) above 200, compared to PSMA negative-control PPC-1 cells and control EL4 cells treated with mRNA encapsulated in separate LNPs (MFIs below 80). The highest MFI was observed in the positive control LNCaP cells (MFI of 435.3) (Fig. 2C and SI Appendix, Fig. S6B). The cell cohorts were then incubated with radiolabeled PSMA-ligand, 68Ga-PSMA-617, and radioactivity in the cell samples was then counted (Fig. 2D and SI Appendix, Fig. S7 A and B). The concentration of radioactivity was 19.56 μCi/mL, a level that had no adverse effect on T cell viability after 1 h incubation (SI Appendix, Fig. S7C) and has not been reported to produce radiotoxicity to T cells (30 μCi/mL for 2 h incubation) (42). EL4 cells treated with LNPs coencapsulating both mRNAs or mPSMA alone had significantly higher 68Ga counts per minute (CPM) per gram of total protein (6.6 and 10.3, respectively, both P < 0.0001), compared to the IgG LNP-treated EL4 cells and PPC-1 cells, while the radioactivity was greatest in LNCaP cells (Fig. 2E).

Based on the consistency of the PSMA expression levels and in vitro radioactivity, tracking of PSMA-tagged T cells with 68Ga-PSMA-617 was assessed in vivo with PET/CT imaging. Naïve BALB/c mice treated with LNPs received an i.v. injection of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (approximately 7.4 MBq per mouse), and whole-body static PET and CT scanning were performed at 2 h post injection (Fig. 2F). Increased 68Ga-PSMA-617 signal was detected in the spleens of the aCD5 LNP-mPSMA group, but not in the NTC or IgG control groups (Fig. 2G). The radioactive dose of the spleen in this study was 8.7 μCi/cc, which did not reduce T cell viability. The 68Ga-PSMA-617 signal was also detected in the kidney and bladder due to clearance through these organs. The tissues were harvested for ex vivo PET/CT imaging followed by gamma counting. aCD5 LNP-mPSMA-treated mice had higher spleen accumulation [0.36% Injected Dose (ID)/g vs. 0.16%ID/g in IgG LNP, P = 0.0265; and 0.14%ID/g in NTC, P = 0.0305]. In contrast, liver accumulation was significantly lower (0.13%ID/g vs. 0.29%ID/g in IgG LNP, P = 0.0401) (Fig. 2 H and I). The lymph nodes from the aCD5 LNP-mPSMA group had the highest 68Ga accumulation (3.78%ID/g vs. in 0.33%ID/g in IgG LNP, P = 0.0455) (Fig. 2J).

Thus, in situ T cell transfection in the spleen and lymph nodes of BALB/c mice by aCD5 LNPs was confirmed by PSMA-targeted PET imaging, whereas nontargeted IgG LNP treatment resulted in liver transfection. This transfection and imaging strategy using aCD5 LNPs and PET was therefore selected for further evaluation and monitoring of CAR-T cell activities in tumor bearing mice.

sec.title: Ex Vivo Validation of In Situ CAR-T Cell Generation in BALB-c Mice.
sec.p: To validate T cell activation and transfection levels, we incubated aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 with freshly isolated murine splenic T cells (SI Appendix, Fig. S8). After 24 h, aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 particles bound to more than 95% of T cells in culture, and 11.0% of T cells expressed CAR19. In the no treatment control (NTC) and IgG LNP-mCAR19 groups, T cell expression of CAR19 was low. We further confirmed the CAR-T functionality via an in vitro assay, and found that aCD5 LNP-generated CAR-T cells eliminated CD19+ A20 tumor cells (A20-WT) but not CD19-knockout A20 cells (A20-KO) (SI Appendix, Fig. S9 A–D). The CAR-T cells had increased lytic A20 cell populations from 15.5 to 52.7% as the ratio of CAR-T cells to A20-WT cells (E:T ratio) rose from 1:2 to 10:1. Killing efficiency of PSMA-tagged CAR-T cells remained after incubating with 19.56 μCi/mL of 68Ga-PSMA-617 for 1 h. The percent of A20-WT-Luc cell death increased from 30.7 to 72.8% as the E:T ratio rose from 1:2 to 10:1 (SI Appendix, Fig. S9 E and F).

We next assessed aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 for generating CAR T cells in naïve BALB/c mice. With IL-7 pretreatment, mice were treated with aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 and spectral flow cytometry of the blood and major organs was performed (Fig. 3A and SI Appendix, Fig. S10). After 24 h, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells as a fraction of CD45+ leukocytes in the spleen decreased by less than 5%, while the populations of other immune cells remained stable (Fig. 3B). For splenic T cells, LNP binding and CAR19 expression were not detected in the NTC or IgG LNP-mCAR19 groups, while aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 bound to approximately 80% of both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells at 5 h, and CAR19 expression increased to 11.6% in CD4+ and 2.8% in CD8+ T cells over 24 h (Fig. 3C). Assuming that approximately 20 million T cells are present in the mouse spleen, with CD4+ and CD8+ T cells constituting about 55% and 45% of this population, respectively, this in situ CAR-T cell generation process would yield roughly 2.5 million CD4+ CAR-T cells and 0.6 million CD8+ CAR-T cells. In murine models, ex vivo engineered CAR-T cell treatments typically require 1 to 5 million CAR-T cells for infusion (43–45), indicating that the number of CAR-T cells generated in this study should be sufficient for effective CAR-T cell therapy against B cell lymphoma. Additionally, approximately 60% of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were activated (CD69+ populations) in response to aCD5 LNP treatment at either 5 or 24 h, compared with less than 20% in the IgG LNP-mCAR19 or NTC groups (Fig. 3 D and E). T cell activation was also associated with elevated CAR19 expression (Fig. 3F).

sec.p: With treatment by aCD5 LNP-mCAR19, CAR19 expression was predominantly observed in splenic T cells and was low in other immune cells, including B cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells (DCs) (Fig. 3G and SI Appendix, Fig. S11). Among all Flag tag+ leukocytes in the aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 treatment group at 24 h, CAR19 expression was observed in 89.9% of CD4+ T cells and 7.2% of CD8+ T cells (Fig. 3H). Alternatively, CAR19 expression in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was detected across various organs and blood, with the highest levels in the spleen (Fig. 3I and SI Appendix, Fig. S12).
Taken together, our image-based data provide proof-of-principle that LNPs can preferentially transfect and create CAR-T cells in the spleen of naïve mice.

sec.title: Ex Vivo Analysis of B Cell Lymphoma Suggests Multiple LNP Doses Enhances Tumor Localization of CAR-T Cells.
sec.p: In situ CAR-T cell engineering was then studied in the syngeneic A20 B cell lymphoma mouse model. Subcutaneous CD19+ A20 tumors were established in BALB/c mice and were treated with aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 (Fig. 4A). Infiltration of T cells and other immune cells increased within the tumors of aCD5 LNP-mCAR19-treated mice over 48 h, compared to the NTC and IgG LNP control groups (Fig. 4B). As analyzed by ex vivo tumor spectral flow cytometry at 48 h post injection, the fraction of dead tumor cells increased from 14.1 to 48.5% (P = 0.0003) in aCD5 LNP-mCAR19-treated mice, while the tumor dead cell fraction was 9.2% and 5.9% in the NTC and IgG LNP groups, respectively (Fig. 4B and SI Appendix, Fig. S13 A and B). The immune cell phenotypes of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were further analyzed (Fig. 4C). The CD3+ T cell fraction was 16.9 and 19.1% in TILs in the NTC and IgG LNP groups, while in the aCD5 LNP group, CD3+ T cells increased to 35.4% (P = 0.0292) at 5 h, 34.4% at 24 h (P = 0.0364), and then slightly decreased to 25.7% at 48 h (Fig. 4D). In addition, plasma was isolated at 24 and 48 h after a single LNP injection and analyzed via a Luminex assay. Chemokines for leukocyte attraction and proinflammatory cytokines were elevated at 24 h (Fig. 4E and SI Appendix, Fig. S14) indicating an immune response, including the infiltration of T cells and other immune cells into the tumor (46).

sec.p: Because mRNA expression is transient and results in limited Flag tag+ T cells in tumors over time (1.9% of CD4+ T cells and 0.2% of CD8+ T cells at 24 h after the first dose), mice were therefore injected with a second dose of aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 at 48 h after the first dose. At 24 h after the second dose, CAR19 expression was 25.9% in CD4+ T cells (P < 0.0001 vs. NTC) and 1.4% in CD8+ T cells (P = 0.0009 vs. NTC) (Fig. 4 F–H and SI Appendix, Fig. S13 C–E). Furthermore, cells with positive Flag tag staining were identified via IHC in tumor samples from aCD5 LNP-mCAR19-treated mice, appearing predominantly at the boundary of the necrotic and viable tumor regions (Fig. 4I and SI Appendix, Fig. S15). Additionally, CTLA-4 and PD-1 expression in splenic T cells was less than 3% of the T cell population after aCD5 LNP treatment (SI Appendix, Fig. S16 A–C). In the aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 treatment group, the effector memory T cells (TEM, CD44+/CD62L−) and the central memory T cells (TCM, CD44+/CD62L+) increased significantly (SI Appendix, Fig. S17). Therefore, T cell memory function improved, and T cell exhaustion was minimal following aCD5 LNP treatment.

In summary, in situ generated CAR-T cells were detected within tumors after two doses of aCD5 LNP-mCAR19. Circulating cytokine levels decreased at 48 h after LNP administration, and therefore this interval was selected for safe repeated dosage. Furthermore, this system of IL-7 pretreatment and aCD5 LNP was safe for repeated administration in in situ CAR-T cell therapy.

sec.title: Bioluminescence Imaging Confirms the Generation and Tumor Infiltration of In Situ Generated CAR-T Cells.
sec.p: BLI was then used to validate T cell migration to tumors following the first dose of LNPs. To track the generation, migration and tumor infiltration of in situ generated CAR-T cells, aCD5 LNPs encapsulating mCAR19 and mFLuc in place of mPSMA were prepared for in vivo BLI. The specificity of CAR19 to CD19+ B cell lymphoma was also investigated by comparing efficacy of aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 with an aCD5-targeted LNP encapsulating identical mRNA with a stop codon (mSTOP) prior to the CAR-T functionality (denoted aCD5 LNP-Mock). A20 tumor bearing mice were treated with 1) aCD5 LNP containing mCAR19 and the mRNA for the reporter gene FLuc, mFLuc (aCD5 LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc), 2) IgG LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc and 3) aCD5 LNP-Mock (-mSTOP/mFLuc) (SI Appendix, Table S7 and Fig. 5 A and B). Based on the in vivo BLI in both the aCD5 LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc and aCD5 LNP-Mock treatment groups (Fig. 5C and SI Appendix, Fig. S18), following the first LNP dose, the bioluminescence signal appeared primarily in the spleen, thymus, and lymph nodes, including the inguinal and tumor draining lymph nodes. For mice treated with IgG LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc, luminescence was primarily observed in the liver. The bioluminescence signal peaked at 5 h and decreased at 24 h.

sec.p: Treatment was then repeated, and at 5 h after the second LNP dose, the tumor luminescence increased in aCD5 LNP-mCAR19/ mFLuc-treated mice, but not in aCD5 LNP-Mock or IgG LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc treated mice (Fig. 5 D and E). In the IgG LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc group, luminescence was again primarily seen in the liver, while in the aCD5 LNP-Mock group, the luminescence was observed in the lymphoid organs but not in the tumors and peaked at 5 h. The bioluminescence distribution was confirmed ex vivo (Fig. 5 C and E).

Therefore, by incorporating a reporter gene into aCD5 LNP-mCAR19, in situ generated CAR-T cells with Fluc tags were tracked in the spleen and tumors in vivo using BLI. Additionally, CAR-T cell tumor infiltration was confirmed with IL-7 pretreatment and at least two doses of aCD5 LNP-mCAR19/mFLuc.

sec.title: PET/CT Imaging Quantified In Situ Generated CAR-T Cell Accumulation.
sec.p: In order to quantify CAR-T cell trafficking, we prepared aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 to achieve in situ-engineering of CAR-T cells with PSMA tags, and monitored the tumor infiltration of CAR-T cells using PET/CT imaging of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (Fig. 6 A and B). A20 tumor-bearing mice were treated with two doses of LNPs prior to the injection of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (approximately 7.4 MBq per mouse) (Fig. 6B). Circulating 68Ga-PSMA-617 was less than 0.81%ID/cc at 3 h after injection in A20 tumor bearing mice compared to 2.02%ID/cc at 2 h (Fig. 6C), and therefore the 3 h time point was used to evaluate T cell accumulation. Whole-body static PET and CT imaging were performed at 3 h post injection of 68Ga-PSMA-617 and 24 h after the second LNP injection (Fig. 6D). From the PET/CT images, 68Ga-PSMA-617 accumulated in the tumors (white dashed circles) in the aCD5 LNP-mPSMA treatment group to a significantly greater extent than in the control groups (Fig. 6E and SI Appendix, Fig. S19A). The 68Ga-PSMA-617 signal observed in the kidneys and bladder results from the renal clearance of 68Ga-PSMA-617.

sec.p: Tumors and other tissues were harvested for ex vivo PET/CT imaging and gamma counting following in vivo imaging. Mice treated with aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 had higher tumor accumulation (0.78%ID/g), compared to the IgG LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 group (0.46%ID/g, P = 0.0254) and the NTC group (0.09%ID/g, P = 0.0013) (Fig. 6F). No significant differences were identified in radiotracer accumulation between treatment groups in the spleen, liver, or thymus (Fig. 6G and SI Appendix, Fig. S19B). A trend toward enhanced lymph node accumulation, however, was observed with the aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 treatment.

These findings highlight the use of PET imaging of 68Ga-PSMA-617 to track in situ generated CAR-T cells after repeated administration of aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19, confirming the specific migration of CAR-T cells to tumors and the minimization of off-target transfection.

sec.title: Efficacy of In Situ Generated CAR-T Cells in B Cell Lymphoma-Bearing Mice.
sec.p: To assess the safety and antitumor activity of in situ generated CAR-T cells, mice bearing A20 B cell lymphoma underwent one treatment session, involving pretreatment with IL-7 every two days and two doses of LNP over a 48-h interval (SI Appendix, Fig. S20A). Following treatment of A20 B cell lymphoma with systemic aCD5 LNP-mCAR19, tumors exhibited cytolytic activity, characterized by disrupted cellular morphology upon H&E staining, and the area fraction of proliferating cells (Ki67+) decreased to 24.3% as compared with the controls (P < 0.0001). CD4+ and CD8+ cells increased at the viable tumor boundary to 0.15 and 0.18 of the area fractions, respectively (each P < 0.0001 vs. NTC) (Fig. 7 A and B). In the aCD5 LNP-Mock group, the viable tumor fraction was 64.3% (compared to NTC, P = 0.0117) with apoptosis and cellular plasma staining of the intact cell membrane and the relative CD4 and CD8 staining was 0.04 and 0.03 in the tumor region. This partial response may result from the activation and enhanced cytotoxicity of T cells by aCD5 binding, with cytokines from activated T cells. Blood was collected at 48 h after the first treatment session. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase (ALK), cholesterol, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, phosphorus, and glucose were all within normal limits (SI Appendix, Fig. S20 B–E). Therefore, in situ generated CAR-T cells displayed limited toxicity and efficacious antitumor activity in a B cell lymphoma mouse model following repeated treatments of IL-7 and aCD5 LNPs.

sec.p: Next, LNPs were administered every other day in B cell lymphoma bearing mice (n = 8 per group) (SI Appendix, Fig. S21A). In the aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 group, the tumor growth was delayed and suppressed (Fig. 7C and SI Appendix, Fig. S21B). With the repeated doses, tumors in 6 out of 8 mice in the aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 group were undetectable and the tumor burdens of the other 2 mice were well controlled until Day 19. There was no significant difference in tumor growth between the aCD5 LNP-Mock and NTC groups. By Day 69, 75% of the mice in the aCD5 LNP group had achieved tumor-free survival (P < 0.0001 vs. aCD5 LNP-Mock, and P < 0.0001 vs. NTC) (Fig. 7D). The antitumor activity of aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 with multiple administrations was also assessed in a brief study. Administration of aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 led to 100% overall survival as compared with only 25 and 50% for the NTC and aCD5 LNP-Mock groups at day 29 (P = 0.0027 vs. NTC and P = 0.0253 vs. aCD5 LNP-Mock) (SI Appendix, Fig. S22).

In conclusion, aCD5 LNP is a safe and efficient system to codeliver PET reporter and CAR mRNAs to T cells, and PSMA-targeted PET imaging proficiently tracked tumor infiltration of in situ CAR-T cells after repeated administration. Importantly, coencapsulating dual mRNAs in aCD5 LNPs also displayed comparable antitumor activity to ex vivo CD19 CAR-T cell therapy in a B cell lymphoma mouse model with multiple treatments.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In vivo T cell engineering simplifies CAR-T cell production and delivery, and eliminates complex ex vivo processes and lymphodepletion. However, creation of effective anticancer protocols and validation of CAR-T cell transfection and trafficking are challenging. In this preclinical study, bioluminescence and PET imaging were combined to provide a system-level and cellular-level view of transfection and to increase the number of imaging time points. In future human studies, PET imaging should be sufficient to confirm tumor accumulation of engineered CAR-T cells and guide treatment decisions. Here, we developed a protocol using aCD5 LNP transfection system to efficiently codeliver imaging reporter and CAR mRNAs to T cells in situ. Since mRNAs share the same translation mechanism, once internalized into the cytoplasm of T cells, the mRNAs are translated by the host’s ribosomes, ensuring concurrent expression of both the therapeutic protein (e.g., CAR) and the imaging reporter (e.g., Fluc or PSMA). By incorporating both imaging and therapeutic mRNAs within a single LNP, our system also provides flexibility in future clinical studies to administer either mRNA independently or in combination, depending on therapeutic and monitoring needs.

The optimized protocol for in situ CAR-T therapy had significant antitumor activity. With pretreatment by IL-7 and administration of aCD5 LNPs, CAR19 expression was detected in 11.6% of CD4+ and 2.8% of CD8+ T cells. The yield of in situ CAR-T cells in this study was therefore roughly 2.5 million CD4+ CAR-T cells and 0.6 million CD8+ CAR-T cells, comparable to ex vivo engineered CAR-T cell therapy (43–45), which was sufficient for effective therapy against B cell lymphoma. In patients, elevated CAR CD4+:CD8+ ratios were associated with enhanced survival due to IFN-γ production and the efficacy of CD4+ T cells (29, 47). In murine B cell lymphoma models, both aCD5 LNP-mCAR19 and aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 treatments significantly suppressed tumor growth and extended survival. We observed that multiple doses of mRNA achieved a comparable efficacy and reduction in tumor growth to the reported studies using ex vivo CAR-T cell therapy in the lymphoma models with the same implanted A20 tumor cells and similar treatment initiation timing (27, 28).

In addition, our approach did not require B cell depletion to achieve therapeutic benefit. In our study, we did not observe significant normal B cell depletion, which may be expected in the context of in situ CAR-T cell therapy potentially through transient mRNA delivery. Furthermore, CAR-T cells are trafficked to the tumor and inflamed site preferentially and may not persist long enough to deplete all endogenous B cells due to transient mRNA expression. In fact, the syngeneic B cell lymphoma murine model and timing of the start of therapeutic delivery here were similar to that described in refs. 27 and 28. Therefore, codelivery of PET reporter and CAR genes not only facilitates the optimization of gene delivery systems but also allows for the assessment of therapeutic efficacy and safety.

Imaging confirmed efficient transfection of T cells in dense lymphoid organs. PSMA expression was detected with PET/CT imaging of 68Ga-PSMA-617. With the administration of a single dose of aCD5 LNP, CAR-T cells were primarily detected in the spleen and lymph nodes, each of which harbor a high density of T cells, likely serving as the primary site for CAR mRNA uptake and CAR-T cell generation. The first dose resulted in a low concentration of tumor CAR-T cells and enhanced circulating T cell recruitment cytokines and chemokines. After a second dose at 48 h, CAR-T cell density was further enhanced in tumors, suggesting activation and migration. The circulating cytokines and accumulation of CAR-T cells in the tumor further suggest that the initial T cell engineering event in the spleen provided a pool of functional CAR-T cells that subsequently trafficked to the tumor site.

Based on the imaging studies, we optimized several aspects of in situ T cell engineering using aCD5 LNPs. Most importantly, a 3-h interval between the PET probe injection and imaging allowed for clearance of the circulating probe and provided the ability to assess the tumor CAR-T population and search for off-target accumulation. PET imaging confirmed that the CAR-T tumor accumulation was specifically enhanced at the tumor site, rather than in off-target organs. The impact of non–T cell–targeted IgG LNPs was greater in the liver as opposed to the spleen or tumors. Second, the dose was optimized to preferentially transfect T cells in the spleen. Splenic transfection was greater than that in the liver with a dose of 7 µg of mRNA in aCD5 LNPs (in approximately 300 µg lipids and 25 µg of aCD5 antibody). Third, the timing of repeated dosage was optimized. Proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines were greatest at 24 h after LNP injection, and therefore, the 48 h dosing interval was required to minimize toxicity. The ability to repeatedly dose LNPs to enhance CAR-T cell tumor localization suggests a potential therapeutic advantage by sustaining CAR-T cell generation and trafficking, overcoming the limitations of single-dose approaches. In total, up to 18 doses of LNP-mRNA were administered to individual mice without detected toxicity.

Fourth, in situ PET tracer labeling offers low radiotoxicity and avoids impairing the function and viability of T cells. The specific imaging method applied here involves several steps that minimize the radiation exposure to the therapeutic immune cell population. The PSMA tag was generated in situ and by delaying the injection of the PET probe relative to the LNP dose, the radiolabeling of the T cells takes place in the tumor. The relatively low concentration of the tracer in situ (below known limits for T cell toxicity) reduced radioactive dose to T cells as compared with ex vivo labeling of CAR-T cells. Therefore, this approach enables noninvasive tracking of engineered CAR-T cells while maintaining potent antitumor activity.

In the future, several strategies can be employed to enhance therapeutic efficacy, including advanced generations of CAR constructs with costimulatory (i.e., 4-1BB and CD28) and signaling domains, coencapsulation of other therapeutic mRNAs to achieve synergistic efficacy or multigene expression using the CRISPR/Cas system. For analyzing T cell dysfunction, CTLA-4 and PD-1 expression in T cells may be indicative of exhaustion, particularly in chronic or persistent antigen exposure, and can also be transiently upregulated during T cell activation. In the future, a characterization of additional exhaustion-specific markers (e.g., TIM-3, LAG-3, or TOX), functional assays (e.g., cytokine production, proliferation, and cytotoxicity upon restimulation would be desirable (48). Additionally, our study demonstrates that a combined reporter gene can be used to identify and track CAR-T cell by PET imaging techniques, and in future human studies, the probes can be further improved for molecular imaging of gene expression. For example, 68Ga can be substituted with other radiotracers possessing longer half-lives and higher spatial resolution, such as 18F and 64Cu, and provide more detailed assessments of gene expression dynamics in human studies.

Overall, this study presents an efficient and safe system for in situ T cell transfection with limited toxicities resulting from increased dose or hepatotoxicity. This system achieves in situ cotransfection of PSMA and CAR19 in T cells, and establishes a foundation for PSMA-targeted PET imaging of in situ CAR-T cell therapy. It provides a noninvasive and highly specific method to assess in situ CAR-T cell generation, improving anticancer function with repeated administration. This innovative PET-guided therapy holds significant potential for expanding its application to solid tumors and other immune-related diseases.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: Additional methods are included in SI Appendix.

sec.title: mRNA.
sec.p: All mRNAs used in this study, including FLuc mRNA (#L-8102), mCherry mRNA (#L-8103), CAR19 mRNA, STOP mRNA, and PSMA mRNA, were produced by TriLink Biotechnology Inc. A flag tag sequence was encoded in both CAR19 mRNA and STOP mRNA. Modified mRNA transcripts have full substitution of N1-Methyl-Pseudo-U and are capped (Cap 1) using CleanCap® AG. The anti-mouse CD19 CAR construct was a gift from Dr. James Kochendorfer at the National Cancer Institute (49). Development of the tPSMA(N9del) construct was described in refs. 19 and 50. The mRNA designs are included in SI Appendix.

sec.title: LNP-mRNA Preparation and Characterization.
sec.p: Lipids in each of the formulations in SI Appendix, Table S1 were mixed in chloroform and lyophilized. The resulting lipid thin film was reconstituted in ethanol at 10 mg/mL. CleanCap mFLuc, mCherry, mCAR19, mSTOP, or mPSMA (TriLink Biotechnology) was dissolved in 25 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 4.0). LNPs were assembled by mixing the lipid ethanol solution with the nucleic acid sodium acetate buffer solution using a benchtop NanoAssemblr™ (Precision Nanosystems). LNPs were washed with phosphate buffered saline (PBS) in 100 kDa Ultra centrifugal tubes (Amicon Merck Millipore, #UFC810024) by centrifuge (2,000×g, 10 °C). Anti-mouse CD5 Rat Monoclonal Antibody (BioLegend, #100602) was incubated with Bond-Breaker™ TCEP Solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #PI77720) for 30 min at room temperature prior to the incubation with LNPs. The LNPs were conjugated with the antibody/TCEP mixture for 1 h and dialyzed in PBS using a dialysis bag with a molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) of 1,000 kDa (Repligen, # G235037) overnight at 4 °C. LNPs were purified through a spin column of Sepharose® CL-4B (Sigma-Aldrich, #CL4B200). LNPs were concentrated using 100 kDa Ultra centrifugal tubes (2,000×g, 10 °C).

The average hydrodynamic (HD) size, polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta potential (ZP) values of the LNPs were measured using dynamic light scattering (DLS, intensity mode) and electrophoretic light scattering (Zetasizer Nano ZS, Malvern Instruments Ltd.), respectively. The mass of encapsulated mRNA was measured using Quant-iT™ RiboGreen® RNA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #R11490) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Animal Models.
sec.p: Naïve BALB/c mice (male, 6-wk-old, 18 to 20 g) were purchased from Charles River. Syngeneic mouse models with intact immune systems were established for this study. For A20 tumor inoculation in BALB/c mice (male, 6-wk-old, 18 to 20 g), 5 × 105 or 2 × 105 A20 cells were collected and centrifuged (100×g, 5 min, RT). The media were replaced with sterile PBS and Matrigel (Corning, #354234) (1:1 ratio in a total volume of 40 μL of volume) for subcutaneous (s.c.) injection in the left hind leg. The tumors were palpable around Day 9 after inoculation, and tumor sizes were measured using calipers (Neiko Tools, #01407A). All the animal studies were performed in accordance with the regulations of the Administrative Panel for Laboratory Animal Care (APLAC) at Stanford University.

sec.title: In Vivo and Ex Vivo Bioluminescence Imaging (BLI) and Analysis.
sec.p: For studying the targeting delivery and specific mRNA expression of aCD5 LNP-mFLuc in BALB/c naïve mice, mice received intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of IL-7 (STEMCELL Technologies, #78054) (200 ng per mouse) prior to intravenous (i.v.) injection of LNPs (7 µg of mRNA per mouse). The groups were 1) No treatment control (NTC, n = 3); 2) aCD5 LNP-mFLuc (n = 3); 3) IgG LNP-mFLuc (n = 3). At the stated detection timepoints, mice received i.p. injection of D-Luciferin (150 mg/kg) and BLI was performed at a series of timepoints (0, 1, 3, 5, 8, and 24 h) using the LAGO system (Spectral Instruments Imaging). At 5 h and 24 h after LNP treatment, the mice were euthanized according to the Stanford University Administrative Panel on Laboratory Animal Care (APLAC) protocol No. 33354, and tissues (heart, thymus, lung, liver, spleen, skin, muscle, and inguinal lymph nodes) were dissected and placed on black paper for ex vivo BLI.

For studying the generation, migration and tumor infiltration of in situ generated CAR-T cells by aCD5 LNP-mFLuc/mCAR19 in A20 tumor-bearing mice, mice were i.v. injected with LNPs (7 µg of mRNA per mouse). The groups were 1) No treatment control (NTC, n = 3); 2) aCD5 LNP-mFLuc (n = 9); 3) IgG LNP-mFLuc (n = 3); 3) aCD5 LNP-mSTOP (n = 3). At the stated detection timepoints, mice were i.p. injected with D-Luciferin (150 mg/kg) and BLI was performed at a series of timepoints (0, 1, 3, 5, 8, and 24 h after the first or the second dose of LNP) using the LAGO system. At 5 h and 24 h after the second dose of LNP treatment, the mice were euthanized, and tissues (heart, thymus, lung, liver, spleen, skin, muscle, tumor, and inguinal lymph nodes) were dissected and placed on black paper for ex vivo BLI.
The normalization and luminescence intensity quantification for each ROIs in each tissue were analyzed using Aura In Vivo Imaging software (Spectral Instruments Imaging).

sec.title: In Vitro Binding of 68Ga PSMA-617.
sec.p: EL4 cell samples (5 × 105 cells per sample) were treated with various LNPs (1.25 µg mRNA per sample) for 24 h. PSMA+ (LNCaP) and PSMA− (PPC-1) human prostate cancer cells (5 × 105 cells per sample) were used as controls. The 68Ga-PSMA-617-stained groups (n = 3 per group) were 1) NTC; 2) aCD5 LNP-mPSMA; 3) aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19; 4) aCD5 LNP-mPSMA+aCD5 LNP-mCAR19; 5) aCD5 LNP-mCAR19; 6) IgG LNP-mPSMA; 7) IgG LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19; 8) IgG LNP-mPSMA+IgG LNP-mCAR19; 9) IgG LNP-mCAR19; 10) LNCap; 11) PPC-1. The unstained groups (n = 3 per group) were 1) NTC; 2) LNCaP; 3) PPC-1.

Cell samples were placed in a round-bottom polypropylene 96-well plate (Corning, #3879), with 200 μL of FBS-free media. The plate was centrifuged (300×g, 5 min, 4 °C) and the media were aspirated gently. Cells were resuspended with 68Ga-PSMA-617 solution (radioactivity was ~1.9 μCi in 10 pmol) in 100 μL of PBS. The method for in-house 68Ga labeling of PSMA-617 is detailed in SI Appendix. Cells were incubated at 37 °C for at least 1 h. The plate was then centrifuged (300×g, 5 min, 4 °C) and washed three times with ice-cold PBS. The cell samples were transferred to gamma counter tubes for measuring radioactivity in a gamma counter (WIZARD2).

sec.title: PET/CT Scanning and Analysis.
sec.p: For studying PSMA expression in vivo, BALB/c naïve mice in different groups were i.v. injected with a 68Ga-PSMA-617 dose of approximately 200 μCi/mouse in 200 μL of sterile saline. The treatment groups were 1) NTC (n = 2); 2) aCD5 LNP-mPSMA (n = 3); 3) IgG LNP-mPSMA (n = 3). The four mice used for one scanning session were all from different treatment groups and injected with the radiotracer at the same time. After 2 h, the mice were placed on a custom 3D-printed mouse bed (capacity for four mice) in the PET/CT scanner (Siemens Inveon), and a CT scan followed by a whole-body static PET scan (30-min list mode) was performed for image acquisition. Immediately after the in vivo PET/CT scan, approximately 700 μL of blood was collected, the mice were euthanized, and the tissues (heart, thymus, lung, liver, kidneys, spleen, skin, muscle, and lymph nodes) were dissected for ex vivo PET/CT scanning. The tissues were immersed in PBS and placed in 24-well plates. The plates were then transferred to the PET/CT scanner, and a CT scan followed by a static PET scan (30-min list mode) was performed.

For studying the tumor infiltration of PSMA-tagged CAR-T cells in vivo, A20 tumor-bearing mice in different groups were i.v. injected with a 68Ga-PSMA-617 at a dose of approximately 200 μCi/mouse in 200 μL of sterile saline. The treatment groups were 1) NTC (n = 2); 2) aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 (n = 3); 3) IgG LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19 (n = 3). The four mice used for one scanning session were all from different treatment groups and injected with the radiotracer at the same time. After 3 h, the mice were placed on a custom 3D-printed mouse bed in the PET/CT scanner, and a CT scan followed by a whole-body static PET scan (30-min list mode) was performed. Immediately after the in vivo PET/CT scan, approximately 700 μL of blood was collected, the mice were euthanized, and the tissues (heart, thymus, lung, liver, kidneys, spleen, skin, muscle, tumor, and lymph nodes) were dissected for ex vivo PET/CT scanning. The tissues were immersed in PBS and placed in 24-well plates. The plates were then transferred to the PET/CT scanner, and a CT scan followed by a static PET scan (30-min list mode) was performed.

The image data were reconstructed using 3D ordered-subset expectation maximization using maximum a posteriori (3D-OSEM/MAP) image reconstruction and converted to units of percent injected dose per cubic centimeter (%ID/cc). PET image analysis was performed with Inveon Research Workplace (IRW) software after the coregistration of PET and CT images. After this, maximum intensity projections (MIPs) of the processed images were generated.

sec.title: Biodistribution of 68Ga-PSMA-617.
sec.p: The tissues harvested from the 68Ga-PSMA-617-injected mice, as described above, were transferred from 24-well plates to gamma counter tubes followed by ex vivo PET/CT imaging. To further quantify the amount of 68Ga-PSMA-617, the tissues were weighed, and the radioactivity measurements were normalized to grams of tissues and the decay of 68Ga, and the injected dose of 68Ga-PSMA-617 for each mouse.

sec.title: Luminex Assay for Cytokine Secretion.
sec.p: At 24 and 48 h post LNP administration, approximately 700 μL of blood was collected in EDTA-treated tubes and then centrifuged (1,000×g, 10 min at 4 °C). The isolated plasma samples were stored at 80 °C until analysis. Cytokines were analyzed by the Human Immune Monitoring Center (HIMC) at Stanford University using a mouse 48-plex Luminex assay. Control beads (Radix BioSolutions) as nonspecific binding were included for normalizing data.

sec.title: Survival Study.
sec.p: The A20 tumor mouse model was used for all survival studies. 2.5 × 105 A20 cells in sterile PBS and Matrigel (ratio at 1:1 in total 40 μL of volume) were s.c. injected in the left hind leg of BALB/c mice on Day 0. Pretreatment of IL-7 (200 ng per dose, i.p.) was administered on Day 6 and 8, and then LNPs (10 μg of mRNA per dose, i.v.) were administered starting from Day 9. For aCD5 LNP-mCAR19, each dose contained 10 μg of mCAR19. For aCD5 LNP-mPSMA/mCAR19, each dose contained 5 μg of mPSMA and 5 μg of mCAR19. For the long-term survival studies, consistent doses of IL-7 and LNPs were repeatedly administered every two days from Day 6 and Day 9, respectively. Each mouse received up to 18 doses of LNP-mRNA in total, until Day 43. Tumor width (w) and length (l) was measured by caliper, and the tumor volume was calculated: tumor volume = w2 × l × ½. Mice were euthanized when the tumor diameter reached 17 mm.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses.
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using Prism GraphPad 10 software. Values of P < 0.05 were considered significant and were adjusted for multiple comparisons as indicated in the figure captions. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Analysis of differences between two normally distributed test groups or phenotypes was performed using a Student’s t test (two-tailed). Analysis of the mean of each treatment group was performed by ordinary one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Statistical tests are reported in the relevant figure captions.
